kid.question: What does the Lord promise to do with His people’s sins?

options.text: Write them on stone
Blot them out
Give them to Babylon
Hide them in a box

kid.explanation: Though Israel has wearied the Lord with sins, He promises to blot out transgressions for His own sake.

kid.question: What does the Lord promise to pour on His people’s children?

options.text: Molten silver
Dust from Babylon
His Spirit and blessing
Ashes from idols

kid.explanation: The Lord promises Spirit and blessing to descendants, pictured as water on thirsty ground and willows by streams.

kid.question: What does one person say about belonging to God?

options.text: I belong to Babylon
I made the Lord
I have no name
I am the Lord’s

kid.explanation: The renewed people openly identify themselves with the Lord and with Israel.

kid.question: What does the Lord say about other gods beside Him?

options.text: There is no other God
They are all stronger
They will soon help Israel
They made the earth

kid.explanation: The Lord calls Himself first and last, denies any rival God, and names His people as witnesses.

kid.question: Can the carved image help the people who make it?

options.text: Yes, it can create them
No, it cannot profit them
Yes, it can forgive them
Yes, it can guide every nation

kid.explanation: The makers and devotees of images are themselves limited people; the images cannot profit them.

kid.question: What happens to the smith as he works?

options.text: He creates rain
He stops needing food
He becomes tired and thirsty
He turns into an image

kid.explanation: The smith tires and thirsts while the carpenter measures an image shaped like a human.

kid.question: What else does the person do with the wood used for an idol?

options.text: Plants it in the sea
Builds a prison from it
Uses it to make rain
Burns some to cook food

kid.explanation: The same wood warms a person, cooks food, and becomes an object of worship.

kid.question: What question does the idol maker fail to ask?

options.text: Am I trusting a piece of wood?
Will my food be ready?
Where should I plant a tree?
Who sharpened my axe?

kid.explanation: The idol maker fails to consider the contradiction and is described as feeding on ashes.

kid.question: What does the Lord tell Israel after describing the idols?

options.text: You must make a new image
You are not forgotten
You are beyond return
You should trust the smith

kid.explanation: The Lord tells Israel it is not forgotten and has been redeemed, so it should return and sing.

kid.question: What does the Lord say will happen to Jerusalem?

options.text: It will become an idol
It will sink into the sea
It will be inhabited again
It will remain empty forever

kid.explanation: The Creator promises to rebuild Jerusalem and confirms His messengers’ word.

high-school.question: What contrast gives the forgiveness promise its force?

options.text: The people brought many offerings, so God owes them pardon
God forgets the people while remembering their sins
The people failed to honor God, yet He offers to erase their sins
The people’s sacrifices replaced the need for repentance

high-school.explanation: Though Israel has wearied the Lord with sins, He promises to blot out transgressions for His own sake.

high-school.question: How does the water image explain the promise to descendants?

options.text: The descendants must build irrigation canals first
The promise concerns only physical rain
The children will no longer need guidance
God’s Spirit brings growth where life was dry

high-school.explanation: The Lord promises Spirit and blessing to descendants, pictured as water on thirsty ground and willows by streams.

high-school.question: What does the repeated naming in verse 5 show?

options.text: People willingly claim covenant belonging
Each person is choosing a different god
Names have replaced the need for faith
Israel’s identity is being erased

high-school.explanation: The renewed people openly identify themselves with the Lord and with Israel.

high-school.question: Why are the people called witnesses after the Lord says He is first and last?

options.text: They must prove their own power to foretell events
They can testify to His unique, enduring acts
They are asked to design a better image
They must choose which god created them

high-school.explanation: The Lord calls Himself first and last, denies any rival God, and names His people as witnesses.

high-school.question: Why does Isaiah draw attention to the image makers being human?

options.text: Human skill is forbidden in every setting
The workers are more powerful than God
Their product cannot outrank the makers who depend on God
The image is valuable only before it is finished

high-school.explanation: The makers and devotees of images are themselves limited people; the images cannot profit them.

high-school.question: What does the tired smith reveal about the idol-making process?

options.text: It gives the worker lasting strength
It produces a living helper
It proves the image can create life
It depends on a limited worker

high-school.explanation: The smith tires and thirsts while the carpenter measures an image shaped like a human.

high-school.question: What makes worshipping the leftover wood absurd in Isaiah’s example?

options.text: The same material was ordinary fuel minutes earlier
The wood is too expensive for worship
The idol has moved from its place
The food was cooked without a fire

high-school.explanation: The same wood warms a person, cooks food, and becomes an object of worship.

high-school.question: What is the force of “he feedeth on ashes”?

options.text: He has no ordinary food available
His chosen trust cannot nourish or deliver him
The idol has fed him a meal
He is punished for cooking bread

high-school.explanation: The idol maker fails to consider the contradiction and is described as feeding on ashes.

high-school.question: How does “return unto me; for I have redeemed thee” differ from the idol maker’s prayer?

options.text: The people must first carry God to safety
The image offers forgiveness before it is made
The Lord initiates rescue and invites response
The return depends on the quality of a crafted object

high-school.explanation: The Lord tells Israel it is not forgotten and has been redeemed, so it should return and sing.

high-school.question: Why are creation and Jerusalem’s rebuilding mentioned together?

options.text: Rebuilding a city is identical to creating the heavens
The city must be rebuilt before God can act
Human builders are more reliable than prophets
The One who made all things can accomplish restoration

high-school.explanation: The Creator promises to rebuild Jerusalem and confirms His messengers’ word.

expert.question: Why is “for mine own sake” significant after the catalogue of failed devotion?

options.text: It means God has no concern for the covenant people
It credits Israel’s offerings with earning redemption
It makes forgiveness independent of any divine promise
Pardon rests on God’s gracious purpose rather than Israel’s performance

expert.explanation: Though Israel has wearied the Lord with sins, He promises to blot out transgressions for His own sake.

expert.question: How does the movement from dry ground to willows interpret the Spirit promise?

options.text: Divine blessing changes a vulnerable future into flourishing life
The metaphor restricts the promise to farming families
The children become independent of the Lord once grown
The plants represent the idols Israel must make

expert.explanation: The Lord promises Spirit and blessing to descendants, pictured as water on thirsty ground and willows by streams.

expert.question: How does verse 5 answer the previous promise of Spirit on descendants?

options.text: The descendants reject every connection to Jacob
Renewed identity is publicly embraced by those who receive the blessing
The blessing produces secrecy rather than allegiance
The names are imposed by foreign rulers

expert.explanation: The renewed people openly identify themselves with the Lord and with Israel.

expert.question: How does the “first and last” claim frame the challenge to rival gods?

options.text: It divides history between two equal gods
It restricts divine knowledge to the distant past
The Lord’s comprehensive agency leaves no comparable divine power
It transfers responsibility for the future to witnesses

expert.explanation: The Lord calls Himself first and last, denies any rival God, and names His people as witnesses.

expert.question: What is the argument in calling the image’s makers its witnesses?

options.text: The makers can certify its divine origin
The makers replace Israel as the Lord’s witnesses
The image has no need for any witness
Those who know its human origin expose its inability to save

expert.explanation: The makers and devotees of images are themselves limited people; the images cannot profit them.

expert.question: How do the smith’s fatigue and the carpenter’s measurements sharpen Isaiah’s critique?

options.text: The supposed god is fashioned through ordinary, dependent human labor
The workers are punished for poor craftsmanship
The measurements reveal a divine blueprint
The fatigue shows the image is already powerful

expert.explanation: The smith tires and thirsts while the carpenter measures an image shaped like a human.

expert.question: What logical contradiction does the split log expose?

options.text: A person uses one tree for two crafts
A person treats one part as fuel and the remainder as a savior
Wood can be both strong and flammable
The worker needs both heat and food

expert.explanation: The same wood warms a person, cooks food, and becomes an object of worship.

expert.question: Why does Isaiah emphasize a failure to reflect, not merely a mistaken craft technique?

options.text: A better-shaped image would solve the problem
Only the choice of tree was mistaken
The deeper problem is a deceived judgment that cannot name its own lie
The passage praises the worker’s practical reasoning

expert.explanation: The idol maker fails to consider the contradiction and is described as feeding on ashes.

expert.question: What is the causal order in the invitation to return and the call to cosmic praise?

options.text: Israel’s song purchases redemption
The mountains forgive Israel before the Lord acts
The idol maker’s insight produces the praise
God’s redeeming act grounds both Israel’s return and creation’s song

expert.explanation: The Lord tells Israel it is not forgotten and has been redeemed, so it should return and sing.

expert.question: How does the Creator’s self-description support the promise about ruined cities?

options.text: His independent creative power underwrites His word of restoration
It implies He needs diviners to predict the work
It makes the city’s future depend on idol makers
It means only the heavens, not the city, matter

expert.explanation: The Creator promises to rebuild Jerusalem and confirms His messengers’ word.
